« Pendant deux ans et demi, mon fils a é: “For two and a half years, my son was the punching bag at that school,” Asha says right off the bat. For her two children, who are Black, elementary school was not a place where they were safe, to the point that she decided to homeschool them. Racist incidents, bullying, physical assaults: from 2015 to 2018, at Saint-Clément-Est elementary school and Académie Saint-Clément, in Mount Royal, they went through the worst. The harassment began with racist insults hurled by other students. Elias, her son, was then attacked several times. In one incident with a classmate, he was seriously injured in the eye. He was eight years old.
« J’ai eu peur de le perdre tellement le: “I was afraid of losing him, the attacks were getting so bad,” the mother laments. The nightmare her son lived through from Grade 1 to Grade 3 left scars. “It happened when he was too young. He suffered a lot, it left a trauma that hasn’t been resolved,” she says from her home in Montréal. For Elias, the incidents kept piling up, and the situation got so bad that in 2017, Asha pulled him out of Saint-Clément-Est school to homeschool him. She repeatedly informed the school administration that her children were victims of racism, to no avail. The school board was also asked to step in, without success.
Les choses vont de mal en pis. Ines*, la: Things went from bad to worse. Ines*, Asha’s daughter, was also a victim of racist harassment at school; her attitude was blamed too. In 2018, her teacher handed her an assignment containing the N-word, asking her to come up with variations of the term. The Grade 6 students talked about the exercise among themselves. “Some of them weren’t comfortable, they couldn’t or didn’t dare write anything,” says the children’s mother.
« Ça a amené une discussion. Il y en a q: “It sparked a discussion. Some of them understood clearly that you don’t do that, that it wasn’t a harmless word, that it was insulting,” she says. Asha decided to file a complaint with the Human Rights Commission. Last fall, she won her case. A story that keeps repeating itself Asha’s story unfortunately resembles that of Adrienne Charles, another mother of two. In her case, the events began in 2016 at McCaig elementary school in Rosemère, where Joel* and Avery* faced racist insults from their classmates: “poop face,” “Nutella,” comparisons to gorillas and more. “In a math class, someone addressed my son using the N-word out loud in front of the whole class,” says Ms. Charles. “He started crying.”
Malgré les nombreux signalements à l’éco: Despite numerous reports to the school, then to the Sir Wilfrid Laurier School Board, the situation got worse until 2019. “It completely destroyed their self-esteem. The effect is real, and even today, I have to work with my sons to help them live with it. There are a lot of scars,” laments Ms. Charles, who herself suffered a severe depression. “It destroys family life, it destroys parents.” The family’s troubles are not over. Adrienne Charles must continue to send her children to school, “the lions’ den,” as she calls it.
Joel, l’aîné, est au secondaire, alors q: Joel, the older one, is in high school, while Avery is still in elementary school. “I knew what they were facing, but could I do more than go to the school administration and the school board?” she asks. She denounces wilful blindness on their part, saying they refused to act, citing “isolated incidents.”
<strong>‍</strong>Dans le dossier d’Elia: ‍In Elias’s case, a decision handed down by the Human Rights Commission reveals that the young boy was allegedly treated differently when it came to disciplinary measures: he was reportedly punished severely, while the involvement of other children was downplayed. Losing outdoor privileges, notes in his agenda, parents being summoned, writing letters of apology to children he had defended himself against – his mother lists the various ways her son was reprimanded.
« Les autres élèves n’avaient pas à écri: “The other students didn’t have to write letters of apology, on the pretext that they weren’t mature enough,” she points out. The mother believes this situation echoes several studies conducted over the past 10 years showing that Black children, especially boys, are far more likely to be punished at school. An inequity rooted in the racial prejudice that affects racialized students.
Selon les recherches, ces sanctions disc: According to research, these excessive disciplinary sanctions can then have negative consequences on young people’s lives, including run-ins with the justice system, a phenomenon known in the English-speaking world as the “school-to-prison pipeline,” that is, a path leading young people “from school to prison.”
« Selon les stéréotypes racistes, les ga: “According to racist stereotypes, Black boys are supposedly restless, even impulsive, and not intelligent,” says Asha. A school administrator even allegedly told her son he would end up in prison at 14. Asha laments that her children, especially her youngest, were seen as problem kids who needed to change their attitude. Dr. Sonia Ben Soltane, an assistant professor at the University of Ottawa’s School of Social Work and a specialist in anti-oppressive and anti-racist practices and interventions in social work, notes that racialized children often face a double standard.
« Les mauvais comportements d’un enfant: “A child’s bad behaviour is often the expression of distress; we forget that in the case of racialized children,” she explains. “They are also often treated like adults. When you’re a racialized person, you don’t have the right to make mistakes, you don’t have the right to get angry; you always have to be impeccable.”
<strong>‍</strong>« Je ne connaissais pa: ‍“I didn’t know my rights as a parent, or the resources, or that CRARR existed, or that I could homeschool my children if they were in danger,” says Asha, who laments the lack of resources dedicated to children going through difficult situations at school. The mother does thank the Association québécoise pour l’éducation à domicile (AQED), whose support was a great help. When she chose to pull her eight-year-old son out of school, her decision was met with vehement opposition from the school, which tried to dissuade her.
« Comme ils n’acceptent pas la scolarisa: “Since they don’t accept homeschooling, they sent in the DPJ, Quebec’s youth protection agency,” she says. Asha met with an investigator twice before the file was closed. “The DPJ was used as a tool to intensify the harassment and increase our stress,” she says. “Children aren’t only mistreated in families, there is also mistreatment at school! Why isn’t there a service to report that kind of abuse?”
<strong>‍</strong>En discutant avec d’au: ‍Through conversations with other families who also pulled their children out of school, Asha realized that many children experience bullying. Under the Education Act, every school must have an anti-bullying plan. According to Alex, a Grade 3 teacher, it is an issue that is very present in school culture. “We should be at the stage of having that for racial discrimination,” he adds. “I think that in schools, the perception is still that racism is subjective, that it isn’t systemic.” Rachel, who has been a teacher for 12 years, agrees.
« J’ai souvent l’impression que, pour d’: “I often feel that for forms of bullying other than racism, things are taken into consideration more promptly,” she says. “There is a lack of consistency in interventions and in the strength of the response. Especially when it comes to racially motivated bullying, we aren’t well equipped or supported enough,” she believes. Both teachers feel that school staff lack understanding of race-related issues. There are no statistics on the percentage of racialized staff members in schools, but Rachel and Alex find their professional environment quite homogeneous.
« Ce qui me frappe, c’est que même si la: “What strikes me is that even though the student population is becoming more diverse, the core of Montréal teachers remains very white,” says Rachel. “There is an underrepresentation among staff, particularly in management positions,” adds Alex. To raise awareness among his students, he addresses issues of diversity and racism in his classes, in an age-appropriate way. He and Rachel believe teachers should be trained. “We need to talk about anti-racist teaching in initial training,” says Rachel, who believes there should also be mandatory continuing education on the subject.
« Avec des collègues visés par la loi 21: “With colleagues affected by Bill 21, we worked very hard for a year to get an anti-racism committee in the union, which is one of the possible solutions we could consider,” Alex says. He also thinks that a rethink of pedagogy is needed. “The government is adding professional competencies and revising content to pay more attention to Indigenous realities,” he says of the measure, which he supports. “But I think there is a refusal to do the same for other racialized communities.”

<strong>‍</strong>Mme Ben Soltane recuei: ‍Ms. Ben Soltane collects testimonies on this subject as part of her work. “In my practice, what I’m told about is what children experience in the schoolyard and the classroom at the hands of other children, but also the inertia of staff.”
Outre la difficulté qu’un enfant d’âge s: Besides the difficulty a school-age child may have in reporting incidents, the way the authorities in charge handle the situation can be problematic. “Racist or race-based aggression is downplayed, because people imagine that children don’t grasp the impact of their words,” Sonia Ben Soltane points out.
Alex en constate les effets dans la cour: Alex sees the effects in the schoolyard. “The burden is heavy for racialized students,” he says. “The question gets turned back on them, asking them to prove that the other child behaved badly.” The discussion often centres on how the child reacts rather than on what they are going through. Moreover, adults sometimes recreate these power dynamics.
« Ça peut venir du personnel. Il y a un: “It can come from staff. There is a kind of racism that is very typical of these environments,” says Ms. Ben Soltane. Rachel and Alex regularly hear discriminatory remarks about racialized parents or staff members from their colleagues. “There are stereotypes that remain really present,” says Alex. “In my opinion, administrators and teachers are more suspicious and less patient with Black, Arab and Latino parents,” he admits. “I have my own biases to deconstruct. I am confronted with my own prejudices about parents.”
En 2018, en allant chercher ses enfants: In 2018, while picking up her children from school, Ariane witnessed a serious incident when a student attacked her nine-year-old daughter with a bladed weapon on the grounds of a CSMB school. Besides the seriousness of the attack, which forced staff on site to call the police, the mother laments the way she was treated by the school. “I felt prejudice from the adults, including in the way the events were handled,” says Ariane, whose three children were attending the elementary school at the time.
« On m’a demandé si j’avais de la famill: “I was asked if I had family in Rivière-des-Prairies or Montréal-Nord, when my family has lived in this neighbourhood since the 1970s,” she says. In discussions with the administration, the mother also avoids raising her voice. “I don’t get angry, not because I’m not capable of it, but because I’m a Black woman and if I get worked up, it will escalate and be used against me.” For her part, Asha also believes that being a racialized, single mother tipped the scales. “I’m all alone taking care of the children, and they knew that,” she says.
Mme Ben Soltane estime que, même si beau: Ms. Ben Soltane believes that even though a lot of prejudice persists in schools, things are changing. “In some circles there is growing awareness of the racial and cultural prejudice against certain children and their families, and of the impact this has on young people’s well-being, the quality of service and how they experience certain difficult situations, for example being reported to the DPJ. The Laurent Commission gives us a broader view of the situation, including in other institutions such as hospitals and youth protection.”
<strong>‍</strong>Deux ans après les évé: ‍Two years after the events, following a complaint filed with the Human Rights Commission through the Centre de recherche-action sur les relations raciales (CRARR), the Commission scolaire Marguerite-Bourgeoys, now the Centre de services scolaire Marguerite-Bourgeoys (CSSMB), was ordered to pay $65,000 to Asha’s family for moral damages. The CSSMB must also prepare an anti-racism plan, including training on discrimination and racism.
Celle-ci sera assurée par un expert en l: The training will be delivered by an expert in the field and must be completed by staff within a year. Under the Education Act, every school must have a plan to combat bullying and violence. The plan for the two schools in question, Saint-Clément-Est and Académie Saint-Clément, deemed ineffective, will have to be revised. Their teaching materials will also be reviewed, a decision the children’s mother welcomes. The evidence states that Ines’s teacher lacked sensitivity and trivialized the use of the N-word.
Il est également dit que la commission s: It also states that the school board failed in its duty by not taking the necessary measures to correct the problem. It also notes that school authorities did not take the necessary steps to reassure Asha’s children, in addition to blaming her son and downplaying the facts. Following the complaint filed by Adrienne Charles and CRARR, the Human Rights Commission is also asking the Sir Wilfrid Laurier School Board and the children’s elementary school to jointly pay the family $30,000 in moral damages. The plan to combat bullying and harassment at school, which sanctions racist incidents, must also be circulated to all staff and students. Training must also be offered to staff. “It’s a step in the right direction,” says Ms. Charles.
Je suis déçue que la commission scolaire: I’m disappointed that the school board doesn’t want to comply. I will continue this fight,” she says. Asha also hopes to see change take place in the school system.
